lessons.title: How the Fiscal Deficit Feeds Into Bond Yields and Inflation

body.text: A fiscal deficit is not a number that sits quietly in a government ledger. It has to be funded, and how it gets funded is exactly what shows up, a few weeks later, in your bond fund's NAV, and eventually, if left unchecked, in your grocery bill.

children.text: Three Ways to Measure the Deficit, and Why the Difference Matters

markDefs.definition: Fiscal deficit: total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. The headline number that gets funded through market borrowing and other financing sources.

Revenue deficit: revenue expenditure (day-to-day running costs, salaries, subsidies, interest payments) minus revenue receipts. A high revenue deficit means the government is borrowing to fund consumption, not asset creation.
Primary deficit: fiscal deficit minus interest payments on past borrowing. It strips out the cost of servicing old debt and shows the deficit generated by this year's decisions alone.

children.text: Financial media reports one number, the

A country can have a shrinking primary deficit and still see its total fiscal deficit stay elevated, simply because interest payments on a growing debt stock keep rising. That distinction matters enormously for reading whether a fiscal consolidation path is genuinely sustainable.

body.title: Isolating the Primary Deficit
body.prompt: A government's fiscal deficit for the year is 7.0 lakh crore rupees. Of that, 4.5 lakh crore rupees is interest payments on past borrowing. What is the primary deficit, in lakh crore rupees?
body.explanation: Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments: 7.0 minus 4.5 equals 2.5 lakh crore rupees. A primary deficit this much smaller than the fiscal deficit tells you a large share of this year's borrowing is simply paying interest on old debt, not funding new spending.

children.text: The Supply Channel: More G-Secs, Higher Yields (Usually)

Lesson 1 covered the mechanics: a larger deficit means a larger gross market borrowing programme, which means more G-Secs auctioned through the year. Basic supply and demand takes over from there. If demand for that paper does not keep pace with supply, bond prices fall and yields rise, raising the government's own future borrowing cost and, through the G-Sec yield curve acting as the benchmark for every other rupee-denominated interest rate, raising the cost of capital economy-wide, for corporate bonds, for bank lending rates, and for the discount rate equity analysts apply to future cash flows.

Who actually shows up to buy this supply matters as much as how much supply there is. Banks buy G-Secs partly because SLR requires it and partly by choice, insurers, led by LIC, and pension and provident funds are large long-duration buyers because G-Secs match their long-dated liabilities, and the RBI itself buys and sells through Open Market Operations to smooth the process. For most of the last two decades, foreign investors were a small, capped share of this buyer base.

body.label: India's JPMorgan GBI-EM index inclusion
body.context: India's G-Secs were added to JPMorgan's benchmark emerging market government bond index, expanding the pool of foreign passive and active debt investors buying G-Secs, a structural demand addition that helps absorb the government's borrowing programme without leaning on yields as hard as before.

body.text: This is why the same fiscal deficit percentage can produce very different bond market reactions in different years. A widening buyer base, whether from index inclusion, strong insurance flows, or aggressive RBI OMO support, can absorb a large borrowing programme without much yield pressure. A shrinking or hesitant buyer base turns the same deficit number into a much sharper yield move.

children.text: The Demand Channel: How Deficit Spending Feeds Inflation

Bond yields are only half the story. The other channel runs through aggregate demand directly. Government spending, whether on capex or welfare transfers, adds purchasing power into the economy. If that spending lands on an economy with spare capacity, idle factories, underemployed labour, unused credit capacity, growth absorbs it without much price pressure. If it lands on an economy already running close to full capacity, the extra demand shows up as inflation instead, because supply cannot expand fast enough to meet it.

body.title: Stimulus at the Wrong Time
body.scenario: A government announces a large, front-loaded capex and welfare package late in a fiscal year when capacity utilisation across manufacturing is already running near decade highs, credit growth is strong, and CPI inflation is sitting close to the upper end of the RBI's tolerance band.
body.prompt: Why is the inflation risk from this stimulus higher now than it would have been two years earlier, when the economy had significant spare capacity coming out of a slowdown?
body.modelAnswer: With capacity utilisation already high and credit growth strong, the economy has little slack left to absorb extra demand through higher output. The additional government spending is more likely to bid up prices for the same limited supply of goods, materials and skilled labour rather than call forth meaningfully more production. Two years earlier, with significant spare capacity, the same stimulus would have been absorbed largely through higher output and employment with much less inflationary pass-through. This is exactly why the MPC watches capacity utilisation and credit growth data alongside the Budget, not the Budget in isolation.

children.text: Debt-to-GDP and the Long-Run Yield Story

Even when a single year's deficit is well absorbed, persistent deficits compound into a rising debt-to-GDP ratio, and that number drives a separate, slower-moving channel into yields: the sovereign risk premium. Rating agencies and long-horizon bond investors price in the probability, however small, that a government's debt burden becomes difficult to service or roll over, and that probability shows up as a few extra basis points of yield demanded on every auction, persistently, rather than as a one-day spike.

columns.label: Traditional (textbook Keynesian) view
points: Deficit spending directly raises aggregate demand in the short run
Households and businesses respond to current income and spending, not future tax liabilities
This is the working assumption behind most day-to-day market reaction to fiscal announcements

columns.label: Ricardian equivalence view
points: Rational households anticipate that today's deficit means higher taxes later, and raise savings now to prepare
In its strict form, deficit-financed spending has little net effect on aggregate demand, since private saving offsets it
Evidence is mixed; most economists treat it as a partial effect at best, not a reason to ignore fiscal signals entirely

body.title: Supply Channel or Demand Channel?
body.question: 10-year G-Sec yields rise sharply in the days after a Budget, even though the fiscal deficit target itself came in below the street's expectations. Inflation data released the same week was benign. What is the most likely driver of the yield move?
options: The demand channel: higher expected inflation from fiscal stimulus is pushing yields up

The supply channel: the gross market borrowing figure, or the composition of financing (for instance a smaller-than-expected disinvestment assumption), likely came in higher than expected even though the deficit percentage did not
Yields cannot rise if the fiscal deficit target beats expectations, so this scenario is inconsistent
This must be driven entirely by global bond markets, since domestic fiscal data cannot explain it
body.explanation: With inflation data benign, the demand-pull inflation channel is not the likely driver here. When the deficit itself looks fine but yields still rise, the usual explanation is the supply and financing mix, a higher gross borrowing number than expected, or financing assumptions (like disinvestment or small savings) that push a larger share of the same deficit onto the market borrowing programme, exactly the mechanic covered in Lesson 1's quiz on this same distinction.

body.title: Assessing Deficit-Driven Yield and Inflation Risk
steps: Check the primary deficit, not just the headline fiscal deficit, to see how much of the borrowing is genuinely new versus legacy interest servicing
Check the gross market borrowing number against street estimates, since this drives the supply channel more directly than the deficit percentage
Check where capacity utilisation and credit growth stand, since that determines how much of any stimulus becomes inflation versus output
Check whether the buyer base for G-Secs is expanding (FPI flows, insurance demand) or shrinking, since that determines how much yield pressure a given borrowing number produces
Track the debt-to-GDP trend over multiple years, not just one Budget, for the slower-moving sovereign risk premium channel

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It is educational content on the transmission mechanics linking fiscal deficits to bond yields and inflation, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform.

points: The fiscal deficit, revenue deficit and primary deficit each answer a different question, and professionals read all three, not just the headline figure
Bond yields respond to the supply of G-Secs relative to demand; the same deficit percentage can move yields very differently depending on who is buying
India's 2024 inclusion in JPMorgan's emerging market bond index structurally expanded the foreign buyer base for G-Secs
Deficit spending feeds inflation mainly when it lands on an economy with little spare capacity left, which is why the MPC watches capacity utilisation and credit growth alongside the Budget
Persistent deficits raise debt-to-GDP, which drives a slower-moving sovereign risk premium into yields separate from any single year's borrowing number
